item.title: Programmable functional RNA design with a virtual scientist.
item.abstract: Programmable functional RNA design is central to synthetic biology and therapeutics, yet both human expertise and existing computational methods struggle to directly program the three-dimensional structures that govern function. Here we introduce RhoAgent, an agentic system that designs RNA candidates and iteratively refines them using experimental feedback. RhoAgent uses RDiff, a diffusion-based generative tool conditioned on base interactions and functional motifs. First, we validate RhoAgent by generating diverse and active ribozymes with only 40-70% sequence similarity to their wild-type counterparts. Second, we enhance the cleavage efficiency of the structurally uncharacterized hovlinc ribozyme by up to sixfold relative to the human-expert-truncated construct. Furthermore, RhoAgent generates a fluorogenic aptamer scaffold that improves fluorescence by 230% relative to the wild-type aptamer. Finally, we design three-dimensional scaffolds that spatially position two distinct functional cores, creating aptamer-based Förster resonance energy transfer systems. This design overcomes a key barrier in compositional RNA design by preserving the binding activities of both components.

item.title: Efficient and Accurate Zero Shot Generation of Symmetric Protein Complexes.
item.abstract: Symmetric organization is a fundamental principle of biomolecular complex assembly. The same principle underlies engineered applications, from vaccine platforms to nanomaterials, making symmetric de novo generation a core capability for computational protein design. We establish a theoretical foundation equating generation of an assembly with underlying symmetry group $G$ to generation within a quotient space over $G$. This directly allows $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant models to generate symmetric structures with minimal distribution shift. With this insight we introduce ZeUS ($\textbf{Ze}$ro-shot $\textbf{U}$nified $\textbf{S}$ymmetrization), a framework that converts any pretrained $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant backbone generative model into an efficient generator of symmetric assemblies with no retraining. ZeUS operates on a single $\textit{canonical subunit}$ and utilizes $\textit{phantom subunits}$ to preserve internal model operations, reducing memory and runtime cost by $\mathcal{O}(|G|)$ for finite groups $G$, compared to a full-complex forward pass. We implement ZeUS for IPA-based models (FrameDiff, FoldFlow) and axial-attention-based RFdiffusion, showing high generation efficiency with minimal degradation to generation quality. We then apply ZeUS to generate symmetric complexes of over $10{,}000$ residues with exact, untruncated attention, a scale previously intractable with any model.

item.title: In Vivo Continuous Evolution Systems: Overview, Principles and Applications.
item.abstract: Traditional in vitro directed evolution is constrained by discrete workflows, high labor demands, and separation from native cellular contexts. In vivo continuous evolution systems overcome these limitations by enabling autonomous and targeted mutagenesis coupled with cellular proliferation. This review outlines the key parts of these systems, including elevated mutation rates (10-5-10-4 substitutions per base), orthogonality, and autonomy. We classify current platforms into some categories: phage-assisted continuous evolution, error-prone polymerase-based DNA replication systems, reverse transcription-driven mutagenesis systems, and deaminase-fusion transcription-coupled mutagenesis systems, detailing their mechanisms, optimization strategies, and applications. Finally, we address technical bottlenecks and emerging directions, including AI-driven component design, automated platforms, expanded host compatibility, and broadened industrial applications, providing a roadmap for advancing continuous evolution technology.

item.title: Engineering Escherichia coli Nissle as a Safe Chassis for the Production of Therapeutic Peptides.
item.abstract: Synthetic biology enables the installation of programable genetic functions in microorganisms, positioning them as versatile platforms for therapeutic applications. However, clinical translation requires chassis organisms that integrate safety, genetic stability, and precise control over the activity. Here, we present an innovative engineering framework for the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle (EcN) that transforms EcN into a safe, efficient, and non-proliferative chassis for therapeutic production. The native EcN plasmids pM1 and pM2 were cured and repurposed to encode two functional modules: a CRISPR-Cas12 chromosome-shredding device that prevents bacterial propagation and a programable circuit for payload expression, thereby generating a non-proliferative therapeutic-producing system. To broaden the range of therapeutic payloads, we developed an artificial-intelligence-guided bioinformatic pipeline to predict anticancer cell-penetrating peptides (ACCPPs). As a proof of concept, a candidate identified through this workflow was produced in the engineered EcN chassis and evaluated in human cell culture for anticancer activity. Collectively, this strategy established a modular platform that integrates computational therapeutic discovery with engineered probiotic production, paving the way for the future development of safer microbial therapies and their clinical applications.

item.title: Augmenting the CATH database: a synthetic protein database for training biophysical-aware inverse folding models.
item.abstract: The three-dimensional structure of proteins is a fundamental determinant of their functional roles; however, biophysical properties such as stability, flexibility, and solubility are also critical for the experimental applicability of designed proteins. The generation of protein sequences capable of folding into a desired three-dimensional structure is known as the protein inverse folding problem and represents one of the fundamental computational challenges in protein engineering because of the vast search space involved. Current deep learning-based inverse folding models effectively learn structure-sequence relationships; however, these models largely overlook biophysical properties such as solubility and stability. This is primarily because these models are predominantly trained on natural protein datasets, and although natural proteins are highly efficient in cellular processes, they may not necessarily represent suitable candidates for experimental applications. In this study, 21,668 protein sequences from the CATH 4.3 database that passed the quality-filtering criteria were subjected to multi-objective optimization for stability, solubility, and flexibility using the Heuristic Metropolis-Hastings Optimization (HMHO) approach, resulting in the construction of a biophysically enriched synthetic protein dataset. To evaluate the effect of the data-centric approach independently of model architecture, the PiFold architecture was kept unchanged, and the baseline model trained on natural CATH sequences (PiFold) was compared with the model retrained on the optimized training data (PiFoldOPT) using natural CATH test sequences that had not been modified by HMHO. In accordance with the primary objective of the study, an initial set of 200 proteins was selected from the natural CATH test set using proportional stratified sampling that preserved the protein length distribution, with the aim of evaluating the biophysical properties of model-generated sequences on a representative test subset. In paired analyses conducted on 155 common proteins successfully designed by both models, PiFoldOPT designs exhibited markedly lower instability index values and higher predicted solubility than PiFold designs ([Formula: see text] for both comparisons; effect sizes [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text], respectively). Furthermore, the proportion of designs classified as stable increased from 65% for PiFold to 81% for PiFoldOPT. To evaluate these biophysical gains together with potential changes in inverse folding performance, sequence-level metrics were also compared on the natural test set. PiFoldOPT maintained sequence recovery performance close to that of the baseline model (0.4270 vs. 0.4286), while showing a limited but systematic reduction in prediction confidence (0.3779 vs. 0.3932). ESM-2-based zero-shot sequence scoring, performed to provide an evaluation independent of the biophysical prediction tools used during optimization, further showed that PiFoldOPT designs achieved more favorable protein language model scores for the majority of proteins. Finally, to evaluate whether the biophysical improvements compromised structural integrity, the initial 200-protein test subset selected using proportional stratified sampling that preserved the protein length distribution was used. Within this subset, 161 proteins for which ESMFold structure predictions were successfully obtained for the natural sequence, the PiFold design, and the PiFoldOPT design were included in the paired structural analysis. To minimize method-dependent comparison bias, all sequences across the three groups were evaluated using the same ESMFold structure prediction protocol. Using structures predicted from the natural sequences as references, PiFold and PiFoldOPT designs exhibited mean TM-scores of 0.784 and 0.792, RMSD values of 2.17 and 2.13 Å, and pLDDT values of 66.34 and 66.37, respectively. In addition to paired statistical comparisons, equivalence and non-inferiority analyses supported that the biophysical gains achieved with PiFoldOPT were not associated with a meaningful loss of predicted three-dimensional structural integrity. Taken together, these results demonstrate that biophysically guided training data enable the design of more stable and soluble protein sequences without modifying the model architecture. These findings reveal that, in protein inverse folding, not only model architecture but also the biophysical composition of the training data is an important determinant of design behavior, and demonstrate that biophysically enriched datasets represent a complementary data-centric strategy for protein design.

item.title: Photo-Activatable RNA Switches for Optical Control of Cell-Free Protein Synthesis.
item.abstract: Programmable RNA switches enable target-dependent regulation of cell-free protein synthesis. Here, we report a photo-activatable RNA switch using photocleavable Lock DNA (pcl-Lock) to enable optical control of in vitro translation. Synthesized by solid-phase methods, pcl-Lock incorporates a coumarin-based photocleavable linker that maintains the RNA switch in an inactive state. Irradiation with 456 nm light cleaves the linker, releasing inhibition and activating translation. Light-triggered activation produced β-galactosidase, yielding approximately 4-fold and 30-fold increases in fluorescence and glucose signals, respectively. Native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis confirms efficient photocleavage of the pcl-Lock strand, while control experiments verify that light-dependent activation does not occur with the Lock strand lacking the photocleavable linker. This strategy enables optical regulation of cell-free protein synthesis and establishes a strategy for integrating photochemical control with programmable gene regulation.

item.title: Programmable Synthetic Condensates to Enhance Circuit Robustness for Improved Bioproduction in Bacillus subtilis.
item.abstract: Genetic circuit reliability is often limited by growth-mediated dilution. However, developing an efficient strategy for maintaining reliable circuit function against dilution effects remains a challenge. Here, we introduce programmable condensates to stabilize circuits in Bacillus subtilis. First, we engineered synthetic condensates and employed RIAD/RIDD peptide pairs to selectively sequester the transcription factor (TF). Spatial recruitment of these TF-filled condensates to target promoters facilitated a significant enhancement in gene expression. By tailoring the physicochemical properties and spatial distribution of the condensates, we substantially reinforced the buffering capacity of the circuits at higher temperatures. As a proof of concept, we harnessed this strategy to significantly improve the bioproduction of alkaline protease and 2'-fucosyllactose, achieving a 109.3% increase in enzyme activity and a 108.9% increase in product titer, respectively. Overall, this work offers a valuable toolkit for B. subtilis applications and a programmable framework for robust circuit redesign in other hosts.

item.title: A Synthetic Promoter Library Spanning a Wide Dynamic Range for Metabolic Pathway Engineering in Zymomonas mobilis.
item.abstract: The limited availability of reliable genetic tools has hindered the engineering of Zymomonas mobilis, a promising bacterium for the sustainable bioproduction of commodity chemicals. Here, we present a synthetic promoter library that enables high-resolution control of gene expression in Z. mobilis. We constructed and characterized 29 promoters spanning the broadest dynamic range reported for this organism to date, and 25 were identified with expression levels higher than the previously reported strongest native constitutive promoter, Pgap, including some up to 15-fold higher. Additionally, a set of strong heterologous and synthetic transcriptional terminators that effectively insulate genetic cassettes was validated in Z. mobilis. Promoters were stable under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, highlighting their robustness in industrially relevant conditions. Surprisingly, all of the promoters identified contained non-canonical promoter element sequences that adhered poorly to the proposed consensus sequences. The promoter library and terminators were integrated into the Type IIS-based, hierarchical start-stop assembly system, facilitating high-throughput construction of multi-cistronic designs. We demonstrate their utility through the rapid construction, testing, and optimization of a 2,3-butanediol biosynthetic pathway. This resource substantially expands the accessible expression space for metabolic engineering in Z. mobilis, supporting precise tuning of multi-step pathways and genetic circuits.

item.title: ORB-TXTL: Cell-Free Expression of Membrane Proteins on Lipid Bilayer-Coated Beads.
item.abstract: Membrane proteins achieve a remarkable range of cellular functions, yet their characterization at high throughputs remains difficult with standard reconstitution methods. Here, we develop on-bead reconstitution into bilayers via cell-free transcription and translation (ORB-TXTL), a platform that uses compositionally tunable lipid bilayer-coated silica beads as scaffolds for cell-free synthesized interacting and integral membrane proteins. ORB-TXTL is fast as it takes only a few hours to integrate membrane proteins onto the beads, which can be extensively washed and seamlessly transferred between reaction buffers to perform assays that are read out by standard laboratory equipment without tagging and sophisticated protocols. We first characterized the lipid interactions of the mechanosensitive channel MscL, then screened 169 Escherichia coli proteins, and identified a systematic dependence of membrane integration efficiency on the number of transmembrane domains. Finally, we functionally reconstituted the E. coli phospholipid synthesis pathway, demonstrating that ORB-TXTL is a tractable and cheap chassis for multienzyme membrane biochemistry.

item.title: Programmable and Dynamic DNA Localisation at Synthetic Cell Membranes.
item.abstract: Spatial and temporal organisation of membrane-associated components is fundamental to cellular signalling, yet remains difficult to engineer in minimal synthetic systems. In synthetic cells, DNA and RNA nanotechnology offer programmable molecular organisation at membranes, while in vitro transcription (IVT) enables gene expression-driven regulation. However, integrating these systems within cell-like compartments, such as giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs), remains challenging due to undesirable interactions between transcription machinery and nucleic acid assemblies. Here, we present a modular strategy that couples in situ RNA production to dynamic DNA localisation at GUV synthetic cell membranes. RNA strands, transcribed within GUVs, function as linkers that recruit DNA-conjugated cargo to lipid membranes, enabling programmable spatial organisation. Using this framework, we achieved reversible membrane localisation through toehold-mediated strand displacement and RNase H-mediated degradation. This work establishes a gene expression-driven platform for programmable and dynamic control of membrane-associated components in synthetic cells, providing a foundation for constructing dynamic signalling assemblies and higher-order cellular behaviours.

item.abstract: Cell-free synthetic biology offers a rapid prototyping environment for molecular diagnostics, yet the utility of these systems is often limited by the slow kinetics and restricted multiplexing capabilities of traditional protein reporters. Using BINOCULARs as toehold switch outputs, we achieve visible readout times of less than 5 min in lateral flow assays, achieving a ≥12-fold increase in speed compared to standard cell-free reporters like β-galactosidase or fluorescent proteins. To demonstrate the utility of this platform, we integrated the bispecific reporters with loop-mediated isothermal amplification and lateral flow assays for the detection of mycoplasma, a common adventitious agent in biomanufacturing. The integrated system demonstrates exceptional sensitivity, achieving a detection limit of 50 genomic copies/mL for mycoplasma and a mammalian internal control. Cell-free assay results were available within 5 min following a 20 min amplification step, and we successfully achieved the simultaneous detection of three distinct targets in a single reaction. Crucially, the platform maintains reliable performance in complex matrices and after lyophilization, making it more accessible for point-of-use applications. Our findings suggest that the modular BINOCULAR architecture can overcome current bottlenecks in cell-free sensing systems, providing a versatile and scalable framework for rapid, point-of-use screening across clinical and industrial applications.

item.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable clinical success in hematological malignancies but remains limited in solid tumors by on-target off-tumor toxicity and the inability to precisely control therapeutic activity within the tumor microenvironment. This protocol presents a workflow for localized, spatiotemporal activation of engineered CAR T cells using focused ultrasound (FUS)-induced hyperthermia. Engineered T cells containing heat shock promoter (HSP)-regulated gene circuits (EchoBack CAR T cells) remain functionally latent until activated by localized hyperthermia. The protocol describes the generation of a subcutaneous prostate cancer mouse model, local subcutaneous administration of EchoBack chimeric antigen receptor T cells proximal to the tumor, accurate alignment of the focused ultrasound transducer, and localized thermal stimulation. A central feature of the workflow is a focused ultrasound system integrated with a closed-loop proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller that continuously adjusts acoustic power using real-time intratumoral temperature measurements obtained with a needle thermocouple. This feedback-controlled approach maintains hyperthermia at approximately 43°C for 15 min while limiting temperature fluctuations. Hardware assembly instructions, software code, and experimental procedures are provided to facilitate reproducible implementation. This protocol enables spatially controlled activation of engineered chimeric antigen receptor T cells within tumors and provides bioengineers and immunologists with a practical platform for investigating ultrasound-responsive synthetic biology and controllable cellular immunotherapies in preclinical mouse models.

item.title: Moss is more: The moss Physcomitrium patens as an ideal chassis for plant synthetic biology.
item.abstract: Physcomitrium patens, commonly known as the spreading earthmoss or Physco, has gained increasing attention as a chassis for synthetic biology in plants. This review explores its advantages over flowering plants traditionally used more often for biotechnology, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and maize, including shorter life cycles and ease to handle experimentally, being haploid, and much higher efficiency for integration of transgenes into its genome by homologous recombination. In addition, Physco's ability to maintain episomes also introduces an additional possibility for transgene expression and manipulation. With these advantageous traits, Physco has already been used for synthetic genomes, recombinant protein production, metabolic engineering and artificial organelle engineering. These applications have been enabled by various toolkits developed for construction of transformation cassettes, DNA and RNA editing, as well as different reporters to allow microscopy imaging or quantification of gene expression. While Physco does have limitations, such as its high number of duplicated genes which can present issues when tweaking of native genes is involved, these certainly do not prevent Physco becoming a useful synthetic biology model for further applications on Earth and future space explorations.

item.title: Gut Delivery of Pentameric GLP-1 Using Genetically Engineered Bacillus subtilis.
item.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and GLP-1 analogs are widely used for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and weight management, but current approaches can be limited by manufacturing complexity, cost, formulation requirements, and the need for repeated administration. Living microbial delivery systems offer a potential strategy for sustained gastrointestinal production of therapeutic peptides, but achieving stable expression, intestinal survival, and biologically relevant systemic exposure remains challenging. Here, we developed an engineered Bacillus subtilis (B. subtilis) spore-based platform for the gastrointestinal delivery of pentameric GLP-1. By leveraging the stress resistance, storage stability, and genetic tractability of B. subtilis, we generated a chromosomally integrated strain that secretes a multimeric GLP-1 construct designed to be processed in the intestine into monomeric GLP-1 peptides. Oral administration of engineered spores resulted in a mean serum GLP-1-related peptide concentration of 20.61 and 23.96 nM on days 3 and 5, respectively, in the first trial and 18.72 and 29.27 nM on days 3 and 7, respectively, in an independent second trial, with minimal detectable signal in green fluorescent protein (GFP) spore-treated controls. Treatment was also associated with preliminary glucose-lowering activity in a fasting-refeeding test. In a longer-term study, engineered spore administration was associated with reduced body weight and adiposity in mice with pre-existing diet-induced obesity, with semaglutide included as a positive pharmacologic benchmark. To improve its translational application, we further generated a marker-free strain that retained probiotic-relevant features of the parental strain, including gastrointestinal stress tolerance, epithelial cell adhesion, and antibiotic susceptibility. These findings provide proof of concept that engineered spore-forming bacteria may serve as a gastrointestinal peptide delivery platform and support further evaluation of this approach in disease-relevant models of metabolic dysfunction.

item.title: Precision CAR-Tregs for autoimmunity: Engineering tissue-adapted immune regulation.
item.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor regulatory T cells (CAR-Tregs) offer a strategy to concentrate immune regulation within diseased tissues while limiting systemic immunosuppression. Their application to autoimmunity, however, introduces design requirements that differ from those in transplantation. Autoimmune lesions are heterogeneous, dynamic, and often shaped by epitope spreading, inflammatory disruption of Treg identity, and a narrow tolerance for off-target immune suppression. Here, we examine CAR-Treg development through four interconnected design requirements: target architecture, context-dependent function, lineage stability and persistence, and clinical control. Target selection must consider not only antigen specificity, but also native presentation, accessibility, tissue distribution, and the ability to support productive CAR engagement. Functional programming is increasingly extending beyond constitutive suppression toward inducible and locally restricted regulatory outputs. Durable activity further depends on maintaining Treg identity under inflammatory and repeated antigenic challenge, requiring coordinated control of FOXP3 expression, receptor signaling, cytokine support, and tissue fitness. Finally, therapeutic activity cannot be inferred from blood persistence alone; tissue localization, local phenotype, target engagement, manufacturability, and reversibility are integral to the pharmacology of these products. Using type 1 diabetes as a benchmark and drawing on evidence from neuroinflammation, inflammatory bowel disease, antibody-mediated autoimmunity, and early clinical development, we show how different targeting and engineering strategies address distinct biological constraints. The emerging principle is that successful autoimmune CAR-Tregs will depend less on maximizing suppressive potency than on matching recognition, function, stability, and persistence to the biology of the affected tissue.
